note: Prepared answers warmed into the spoken-question cache at greeter startup. Each entry must be true of the robot as built, must not claim medical authority, and must read well aloud in one or two sentences. The first-aid entries are ordinary household first aid with a clear escalation cue, never a diagnosis. Common injuries are seeded under several phrasings on purpose: a one-topic-word question only ever matches exactly. Time-sensitive or context-dependent questions are never cached, so none belong here. Written and reviewed by hand; the assistant never edits this file without being asked.

entries.question: What are you?
entries.answer: I am BracketBot, a small at home care companion. I can talk with you, keep track of reminders, and help with simple physical tasks.

entries.question: What can you do?
entries.answer: I can set reminders and keep them running in the background, answer questions out loud, wave, shake hands, give a hug when asked, follow someone slowly, and pick objects up from a table.

entries.question: Are you a doctor?
entries.answer: No, and I will never pretend to be one. I can keep you company and help you remember things, but anything medical belongs with a real clinician.

entries.question: Can you give medical advice?
entries.answer: No. I am a companion, not a medical device, so for anything about health please ask a doctor or nurse.

entries.question: How do reminders work?
entries.answer: When someone asks for a reminder, the time is saved on the robot in a small database, so the countdown keeps running while I do other things, and it survives a restart.

entries.question: How do you stay safe around people?
entries.answer: Every movement is a named action that deterministic safety code checks before any motor is touched. It confirms the robot is upright, checks the depth camera for anything in the way, and one stop command cancels whatever is running.

entries.question: Can a language model move your arms?
entries.answer: No. A model can only request one named action from a fixed allowlist, and separate safety code decides whether that action is allowed to run.

entries.question: How do you see people?
entries.answer: I use a head camera and a depth camera. A local vision model finds people in the picture, and the depth camera tells me how far away things are.

entries.question: Do you record video?
entries.answer: No video or audio is kept by default. Frames are processed on the robot and thrown away, and the vision work runs locally rather than in the cloud.

entries.question: How do you pick objects up?
entries.answer: The depth camera finds the tabletop and the objects sitting on it, then the arm plans a full path to the object and only moves if every step of that path passes the safety checks.

entries.question: How do you follow someone?
entries.answer: The depth camera looks for a person shaped object in front of me and I hold a set distance from it, slowly, stopping if anything gets in the way or if the person is lost.

entries.question: What happens if something goes wrong?
entries.answer: Anyone can press stop, and the robot brings the arms back along the path they came, releases the motors, and returns to balancing. There is also a physical emergency stop, with a person beside it whenever I move.

entries.question: Why are you called Baymax?
entries.answer: Baymax is the inspiration, not a claim. The goal is that calm, gentle way of being with a person, without ever pretending to be a medical professional.

entries.question: Who built you?
entries.answer: A small student team built the software on top of a BracketBot, a two wheeled balancing robot with two arms.

entries.question: Can you hear me?
entries.answer: Yes. I wait for a wake phrase, then listen until you stop speaking, and the speech is transcribed on the robot rather than sent away.

entries.question: How do you balance?
entries.answer: Two wheels and a balance controller keep me upright, the same idea as a segway. If the robot is tipped too far, the safety checks refuse to move the arms at all.

entries.question: What should I do if I cut my finger?
entries.answer: Rinse the cut under cool water, press a clean cloth on it until the bleeding stops, then cover it with a bandage. If it keeps bleeding after ten minutes of pressure, or the cut is deep or gaping, please get medical help.

entries.question: How do I stop bleeding?
entries.answer: Press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing without lifting to peek, and raise the injured part above the heart if you can. If blood soaks through or spurts, call emergency services right away.

entries.question: What should I do if I burn my hand?
entries.answer: Hold the burn under cool running water for about twenty minutes, then cover it loosely with a clean non fluffy cloth. Do not use ice, butter, or ointments, and get medical help for anything bigger than your palm, blistered, or on the face or hands.

entries.question: What should I do about a nosebleed?
entries.answer: Sit upright, lean slightly forward, and pinch the soft part of your nose for ten full minutes without checking. If it has not stopped after twenty minutes or followed a hard blow to the head, please get medical help.

entries.question: What should I do for a sprained ankle?
entries.answer: Rest it, put something cold wrapped in a cloth on it for twenty minutes at a time, wrap it snugly, and keep it raised. If you cannot put weight on it at all or it looks misshapen, please have it looked at.

entries.question: What should I do if someone is choking?
entries.answer: If they cannot speak, cough, or breathe, call emergency services and give firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then abdominal thrusts. If they can still cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing.

entries.question: What should I do about a bee sting?
entries.answer: Scrape the stinger out sideways with something with a firm edge, wash the spot, and use something cold for the swelling. If there is trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or dizziness, call emergency services immediately.

entries.question: What should I do for a headache?
entries.answer: Try water, a rest in a dim quiet room, and the pain reliever you normally use as directed. If it is the worst headache of your life, came on suddenly, or comes with confusion, weakness, or a stiff neck, get help right away.

entries.question: What should I do if I have a fever?
entries.answer: Rest, sip fluids steadily, and dress lightly. Please seek medical care for a fever above thirty nine and a half degrees Celsius, one lasting more than three days, or any fever with a stiff neck, rash, confusion, or trouble breathing.

entries.question: What should I do if I feel dizzy?
entries.answer: Sit or lie down right away so a faint cannot hurt you, and sip some water. If dizziness comes with chest pain, slurred speech, weakness on one side, or a bad headache, call emergency services.

entries.question: How do I get a splinter out?
entries.answer: Wash your hands and the skin, then pull the splinter out along the angle it went in using clean tweezers, and wash again afterwards. If it is deep, under a nail, or will not come out, let a clinician remove it.

entries.question: What should I do for a scrape?
entries.answer: Rinse the scrape with cool running water to get the grit out, pat it dry, and cover it with a clean bandage. Watch for spreading redness, warmth, or pus over the next few days and get it checked if you see them.

entries.question: What should I do about an allergic reaction?
entries.answer: For trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or faintness, use an epinephrine injector if one is prescribed and call emergency services at once. Mild itching or hives alone can usually wait for your regular clinician.

entries.question: When should I call an ambulance?
entries.answer: Call emergency services for chest pain, trouble breathing, heavy bleeding that will not stop, sudden weakness or slurred speech, a seizure, or anyone who cannot be woken. When you are unsure, calling is the right choice.

entries.question: What should I do if someone faints?
entries.answer: Lay them on their back and raise their legs a little, loosen tight clothing, and check that they are breathing. If they do not wake within a minute, or they are not breathing normally, call emergency services.

entries.question: How do I do CPR?
entries.answer: Call emergency services first and put the phone on speaker, then push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second, and let the chest come all the way back up each time. The dispatcher will count with you until help arrives.

entries.question: What should I do about a bruise?
entries.answer: Put something cold wrapped in a cloth on it for twenty minutes at a time for the first day, and keep it raised if you can. Get it checked if the pain is severe, the joint will not move, or bruises keep appearing on their own.

entries.question: What should I do if I hit my head?
entries.answer: Rest, use something cold on the sore spot, and have someone stay nearby for the next day. Get urgent care for vomiting, worsening headache, confusion, one pupil larger than the other, or any loss of consciousness.
